summary:
NASA's fire record changed instruments in 2012. MODIS sees fires in 1 km pixels. VIIRS sees them in 375 m pixels and reports many small fires that MODIS misses. Added together, the raw counts jump from 4.4 million detections in 2011 to 21.9 million in 2012 and 40.5 million in 2024.

blazeBridge puts the whole record on a single scale. It is a web app where you pick a country, state or draw an area, and get its burning activity calendar, whether it is above or below normal for that place and time and presents it all in a digestible, easy to use manner without losing any tools or information.

This matters now. The two MODIS satellites stop in 2027. Without a bridge, 25 years of data stop being comparable with everything that comes after. blazeBridge already keeps its main record in the unit of the newer satellites, so the record can continue with no issue.
details:
The problem. A detection is one satellite pixel with the heat of a fire. VIIRS pixels (375 m) are about seven times smaller in area than MODIS pixels (1 km). So VIIRS sees small fires that MODIS misses, and it splits large fires into more detections. Next to the MODIS years, almost every month since 2012 looks like a record, so “is this month normal?” gets the wrong answer.

What it does. Pick any of 235 countries and territories or a state, draw an area, or type coordinates. You get:

  • a fire calendar of all 312 months since November 2000, with estimated months marked;
  • one sentence comparing the month with its median in 2013–2025, such as “About normal for October”;
  • the season so far, the share of fires seen at night, and fire strength, each compared with normal;
  • the last 7 days ranked by urgency, with industrial heat sources and detections over the sea removed;
  • a confidence map, tested in 7,920 squares of about 100 km;
  • CSV downloads, an open API, and colour scales for colour blindness.

How it works. We learn the conversion from February 2012 to December 2021, when MODIS and VIIRS both flew in their standard orbits. After that, Aqua’s orbit drifts. One global factor fails: for a large forest fire, VIIRS mostly splits the same fire into more pixels, while for small farm burns it adds fires MODIS never saw. So blazeBridge learns a separate ratio for each 5° region (about 550 km across) and calendar month. Aqua passes at the same time of day as VIIRS, so it counts 70 % and Terra 30 %. The unit is NOAA-20 VIIRS detections, because VIIRS keeps flying and new months stay measured. A second view, the strict long record, converts the other way, into what Aqua MODIS would have reported.

Does it work. We hid each of the ten overlap years in turn and rebuilt it from the other nine: 68,436 region-months in total.

  • Per 5° region and month, the estimate is off by 12 %. The global total is within 1 %.
  • Suomi NPP and NOAA-20 carry VIIRS instruments of the same design and still differ by 7 %. That is the floor no method can beat.
  • Bigger areas are more exact: 7 % off for an area about 2,000 km across, 12 % for 600 km, 24 % for 100 km.
  • Why regions matter, from the same test in the VIIRS-to-Aqua direction: raw counts are 513 % off, one global factor 28 %, one ratio per region and month 16 %, and our full conversion 9 %.
  • Months before 2012 cannot be checked directly, and clouds hide fires. The app says so next to every answer.

Who it is for. Fire managers who need to know whether this month is unusual, ecologists who want 26 fire seasons without the false jump, and anyone checking a claim such as “fires went up five times”.

What is new. Most fire maps show where it burns today. blazeBridge says whether that is normal there, and how far to trust the answer, square by square.

Impact. NASA retires MODIS in 2026–27. blazeBridge keeps 26 years of fire history comparable with every VIIRS month that comes next, so fire agencies can keep asking “is this normal?” and get an honest answer. The data is open: anyone can download it or use the API.

What we considered. Satellite timing (Aqua passes at the same time as VIIRS, Terra in the morning), Aqua’s orbit drift after 2021, false fires from industrial heat sources and the sea, clouds that hide fires, colour blindness, and honesty about uncertainty: every answer shows a likely range and how far to trust it.

Tools. Python and DuckDB to process 490 million NASA FIRMS detections, FastAPI for the API, D3 for the globe and charts, hosted on Hugging Face Spaces.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. The idea, the goals and the interface design are ours. Claude (Anthropic) wrote code under our direction and helped edit and format the documentation. This is stated in the project description and in the code repository. No SI-generated images, video or audio.
